5962: Election, grace and the human will
5963: How does God save — election, grace and the human will?
5964:
All the traditions surveyed here agree that salvation is a gift of God's grace in Jesus Christ, that humans are sinners who cannot save themselves, and that faith is necessary. They disagree about how God's eternal choice relates to human response: whether God's election is unconditional or based on foreseen faith, whether grace can be resisted, whether Christ died with the intention of saving every person or a definite people, whether fallen people are able to respond to the gospel, and whether believers can finally fall away.

The debate is ancient (Augustine against Pelagius in the fifth century), was sharpened in the Reformation (Luther against Erasmus, Dort against the Remonstrants, Jesuits against Dominicans), and remains lively today, especially among Baptists and evangelicals. Each position below is presented as its own best advocates would present it, with the strongest objections from the others and the replies they give.
5966:
Calvinism holds that fallen humans are unable, by their own powers, to turn to God, so salvation depends entirely on God's sovereign initiative. Before creation God unconditionally chose a definite people in Christ; Christ's death secures their redemption; the Holy Spirit effectually regenerates them so that they freely and willingly believe; and God preserves them to the end.

The position is usually summarised by the later acronym TULIP (Total depravity, Unconditional election, Limited or particular atonement, Irresistible or effectual grace, Perseverance of the saints), which tracks the five heads of doctrine of the Synod of Dort (1618–1619). Its defenders stress that this framework gives God all the glory, grounds assurance in God's purpose rather than human resolve, and is the most natural reading of Romans 8–9, Ephesians 1 and John 6.
5968: North African bishop whose controversy with Pelagius and his followers produced the Western church's classic doctrines of original sin, the necessity of prevenient and operative grace, and gratuitous predestination. His late anti-Pelagian works argue that both the beginning of faith and perseverance are gifts given to the elect. Later Calvinists regarded him as their chief patristic forebear, though he also held views (on baptismal regeneration and the possibility of regenerate people not persevering) that Reformed theology does not share.
5970: French humanist-trained reformer who led the church in Geneva. His *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, expanded from 1536 to its final Latin edition of 1559, treats election and reprobation in the context of the Christian life and assurance rather than as a starting axiom. He taught that God's eternal decree chose some to life and passed over others, and called the decree of reprobation awe-inspiring yet just. His biblical commentaries remain widely used.
5972: Calvin's successor in Geneva, professor of theology
5973: Beza led the Genevan Academy after Calvin and gave Reformed predestination a more tightly ordered, scholastic presentation, including a chart of the order of the divine decrees. He is often associated with supralapsarianism and with the doctrine of definite atonement. Jacobus Arminius studied under him in Geneva before later breaking with this system.
5975: English Puritan pastor, theologian, Oxford vice-chancellor
5976: The most influential English Puritan theologian. His *Death of Death in the Death of Christ* is the classic defence of particular redemption, arguing that Christ's death actually accomplishes salvation for those for whom it was intended rather than making salvation merely possible. He also wrote a polemic against Arminianism and major works on the Holy Spirit and communion with God.
5978: Presbyterian theologian, founder of Ligonier Ministries
5979: American teacher whose books, lectures and radio broadcasts did much to spread Reformed soteriology among late-twentieth-century evangelicals. His *Chosen by God* explains predestination for lay readers, emphasising regeneration preceding faith and the holiness of God.
5980: The position grew out of Augustine's fifth-century conflict with Pelagianism and was revived in the sixteenth century by the magisterial Reformers, all of whom (Luther included) taught the bondage of the will. In the Reformed churches it was refined in debate: after Arminius's followers issued the Remonstrance (1610), the international Synod of Dort (1618–1619) answered with the Canons of Dort, whose five heads of doctrine are the basis of the later TULIP acronym (the acronym itself is modern, attested only from the early twentieth century). The Westminster Confession (1646) and the London Baptist Confession (1689) embedded the doctrine in Presbyterian and Particular Baptist churches. English and American Puritans, the evangelical leader George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards, Charles Spurgeon, and the twentieth-century 'new Calvinism' associated with figures such as J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul and John Piper carried it into the modern era.
5981: 1. Total depravity: sin affects every part of the person, so that no one, left to themselves, will or can come to God in saving faith (not that people are as wicked as possible).
5982: 2. Unconditional election: before creation God chose particular people for salvation in Christ, not because he foresaw their faith or merit but according to his own good pleasure.
5983: 3. Particular (definite) redemption: Christ's death was intended to secure and actually accomplish the salvation of the elect, while being sufficient in worth for all and sincerely offered to all.
5984: 4. Effectual (irresistible) grace: the Spirit regenerates the elect so that they freely come to Christ; outward calls can be and are resisted, but God's inward call infallibly achieves its purpose.
5985: 5. Perseverance of the saints: those whom God has truly regenerated will be kept by God and will continue in faith to the end, though they may fall seriously for a time.
5986: 6. Compatibilism: God's decree and genuine human choice are both real; humans act willingly and are responsible, though their choices are certain under God's providence.
5987: God chose Jacob over Esau before either had done good or evil, so that his purpose of election would stand; mercy depends on God who shows it, not on human will or effort. Read as individual election to salvation.
5988: The Father chose believers in Christ before the foundation of the world and predestined them to adoption according to the purpose of his will, which works all things according to his counsel.
5989: All whom the Father gives to the Son will come; no one can come unless the Father draws him, and every one who is drawn is raised up on the last day. The drawing is therefore effectual, not merely enabling.
5990: As many as were appointed to eternal life believed: appointment precedes and explains faith.
5991: The golden chain: those foreknown (known in covenant love) are predestined, called, justified and glorified, with no one lost between links.
5992: Jesus tells his opponents they do not believe because they are not his sheep, implying belonging precedes believing.
5993: Humans are dead in sin until God makes them alive with Christ; faith and salvation are God’s gift so that no one may boast.
5994: The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, a particular people (compare John 10:15 and John 17:9).
5995: God who began the good work will bring it to completion, grounding perseverance in God’s faithfulness.
5996: The clearest passages on election (Romans 9, Ephesians 1, John 6) ground salvation in God's choice prior to and independent of human response, and Paul anticipates the objection 'is God unjust?', which would only arise if election were unconditional.
5997: Scripture describes the unregenerate as dead, blind, hostile to God and unable to submit to him, so faith must be the fruit of regeneration rather than its cause.
5998: If two people receive the same grace and one believes while the other does not, the deciding factor lies in the human; this gives grounds for boasting, which Paul excludes.
5999: If Christ's death paid for the sins of all people without exception, either all must be saved or God punishes some sins twice; a definite atonement avoids both by tying Christ's intention to its effect.
6000: Divine foreknowledge of future free acts already makes them certain; Arminian foreknowledge therefore does not remove the difficulty it is meant to solve, whereas a decree explains why the future is certain.
6001: Augustine's anti-Pelagian theology was received by the Western church (Council of Orange, 529, condemned the idea that the beginning of faith comes from human nature), and all the magisterial Reformers affirmed unconditional election in some form.
6002: Assurance and perseverance rest on God's keeping power, which no external power can overturn.
6003: John 3:16 says God so loved the world that whoever believes may have life; this universal love and offer seems incompatible with a decree that leaves most of the world without any provision.
6004: 1 Tim 2:4 says God desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. If God unconditionally elects only some, his stated desire is frustrated by his own decree.
6005: 2 Pet 3:9 says the Lord is not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance. This expresses a universal saving will.
6006: 1 John 2:2 says Christ is the propitiation not only for our sins but for the sins of the whole world, contradicting limited atonement.
6007: Ezek 18:23 and 18:32 (and 33:11) declare that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. A God who passes over people whom he could save appears to contradict this.
6008: In Matt 23:37 Jesus says he often wished to gather Jerusalem's children 'and you would not'. This shows grace can be successfully resisted and that God's desire can be thwarted by human refusal.
6009: Heb 2:9 says Jesus tasted death for everyone, which seems to extend the atonement to every person.
6010: 1 Tim 4:10 calls God the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe. This implies a saving relationship to all that is distinct from, but not opposed to, his relation to believers.
6011: Titus 2:11 says the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people, which fits prevenient grace extended to everyone.
6012: Acts 7:51 has Stephen charge his hearers: you always resist the Holy Spirit. Grace is therefore resistible.
6013: Heb 6:4-6 describes people who were enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit and then fell away. This seems to deny unconditional perseverance.
6014: Rom 11:32 says God has consigned all to disobedience in order that he may have mercy on all. The climax of Romans 9–11 is universal mercy, not selective decree.
6015: Deut 30:19 calls Israel to choose life. A genuine summons to choose implies an ability to respond; otherwise the command is meaningless.
6016: 2 Pet 2:1 speaks of false teachers denying the Master who bought them and bringing destruction on themselves, which implies Christ's purchase extends to some who perish.
6017: John 12:32: Jesus will draw all people to himself when lifted up. If 'draw' in John 6:44 is effectual, John 12:32 would teach universalism; so the drawing must be resistible.
6018: 1 Cor 8:11 and Rom 14:15 warn that a brother 'for whom Christ died' may be destroyed or ruined, which seems inconsistent with both limited atonement and perseverance.
6019: Luke 7:30 says the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God's purpose for themselves. If God's purpose can be rejected, his will is not always effectual.
6020: Calvinism appears to make God the author of sin: if he determines all things, including the fall and every evil choice, it is hard to see how creatures rather than God bear the blame. Middle knowledge preserves sovereignty without such determinism.
6021: Lutheran theology rejects double predestination and the doctrine of definite atonement as rational speculation beyond the revealed promises. The Formula of Concord (Article XI) warns against inferring reprobation from election and directs consciences to Christ in Word and sacrament.
6022: From the Orthodox standpoint the Augustinian framework (inherited guilt, a will so bound that grace must work monergistically) is a Western innovation, foreign to the Greek fathers, who uniformly taught cooperation between divine grace and human freedom.
6023: Calvinism reads the 'dead in sin' metaphor as total inability, but in Scripture spiritual death means separation, and the same Ephesians 2 passage says believers are saved 'through faith', placing faith logically before being made alive.
6024: If God unconditionally decrees who will be saved, the universal offer of the gospel seems insincere, since God offers to the non-elect what he has not intended for them.
6025: Calvinists commonly read 'world' in John as the fallen human order in its rebellion, so the verse magnifies the greatness of God's love for sinners rather than counting every individual; the promise is genuinely to 'whoever believes', and that offer is sincerely made to all. Others (e.g. Amyraldians, or Calvinists such as D. A. Carson) affirm that God has a real general love for all humanity alongside a particular, saving love for the elect.
6026: Two Calvinist replies are common. Some (following Augustine and Owen) read 'all people' as all kinds of people, in context of praying for kings and those in authority (1 Tim 2:1-2). Others (e.g. John Piper in *Are There Two Wills in God?*) accept that 'all' means every person and distinguish God's preceptive will (what he commands and delights in) from his decretive will (what he ordains), noting that every theology must say God permits what he does not desire.
6027: Many Calvinists note that the letter addresses 'you' (believers) and that God is patient toward 'you', so the 'any' may refer to the elect yet to be gathered before the end. Others accept the universal sense and appeal again to the distinction between what God desires in itself and what he wills to bring about.
6028: Owen and many later Calvinists argue 'the whole world' contrasts John's readers with believers among all peoples, echoing John 11:51-52 where Christ dies to gather God's scattered children. Others (e.g. hypothetical universalists within the Reformed tradition) affirm a universal sufficiency and a real offer grounded in the cross while maintaining a special intention for the elect.
6029: Calvin himself commented on Ezekiel 18 by distinguishing God's will as revealed in the call to repentance, which is sincere, from his secret counsel. Calvinists hold that God genuinely delights in repentance and does not delight in death as such, yet may permit and ordain the just judgement of sinners for wider purposes, much as a judge can lament a sentence he justly passes.
6030: Calvinists observe that Jesus addresses the leaders of Jerusalem ('you would not') who prevented 'your children' from being gathered, and they agree that the outward call is resisted constantly. What Calvinism denies is that the Spirit's inward regenerating work fails. The lament also shows Christ's real sorrow over unbelief, which Calvinists affirm.
6031: Many Calvinists point out that the following verses define the 'everyone' as the 'many sons' brought to glory, the 'brothers' and 'the children God has given me' (Heb 2:10-13), so the scope is all of Christ's people. Others accept a universal reference to the sufficiency of his death.
6032: Calvinists commonly take 'Saviour' here in the broader sense of preserver and benefactor (common grace), with 'especially' marking the unique, eternal salvation of believers; some take 'especially' as 'namely'. Either reading avoids universal saving intention.
6033: Calvinists read 'all people' in light of the preceding instructions to older men, women, young men and slaves (Titus 2:1-10): the grace of God has appeared for every class of person. They also note the grace in view trains believers in godliness (Titus 2:12), which describes saving grace already received rather than a universal enabling.
6034: Calvinists agree that the Spirit's work through the external word, prophets and providence is resisted by sinful people all the time; that is what total depravity predicts. The doctrine of effectual calling concerns the Spirit's regenerating work in the heart, which changes the will so that it no longer resists (Ezek 36:26).
6035: Calvinist interpreters offer several readings: (a) the passage describes people who experienced the blessings of the covenant community without genuine regeneration, contrasted with the 'better things that belong to salvation' in Heb 6:9; (b) it is a hypothetical warning God uses as a means to keep the elect persevering. Either way, 1 John 2:19 shows that those who depart reveal they were never truly of the believing community.
6036: Calvinists read Romans 11 as dealing with Jews and Gentiles as groups in redemptive history: both have been shut up under disobedience so that both receive mercy on the same footing. The 'all' corresponds to both peoples, not every individual, since the chapter itself distinguishes the elect remnant from the hardened (Rom 11:5-7).
6037: Calvinists answer that a command reveals duty, not ability (Rom 3:20); Deut 30:6 within the same chapter promises that God will circumcise hearts so that Israel can love him, which is the new-covenant fulfilment Calvinists see in regeneration. God's commands are also the means by which the Spirit works faith in the elect.
6038: Calvinists note that the verse draws on Deut 32:6, where God 'bought' Israel as a nation, and that Peter describes how the false teachers professed to belong to the Lord; the language is that of covenant profession rather than a statement of the atonement's saving intent.
6039: Calvinists point to the setting: Greeks have just asked to see Jesus (John 12:20-23), so 'all' means people of all nations, Jew and Gentile, not every individual. On that reading the drawing remains effectual for those drawn.
6040: Calvinists commonly understand 'destroyed' here as serious spiritual harm or the damage to a weaker believer's faith that Paul warns against, and they treat the language as a description of covenant members in the judgement of charity; the warnings themselves are means by which God preserves his people.
6041: Calvinists answer that 'purpose' (boulē) here refers to God's counsel expressed in John's baptism, his revealed will that they obeyed or refused, not his eternal decree.
6042: The Westminster Confession (3.1) says God ordains whatever comes to pass yet so that he is not the author of sin and the liberty of second causes is established. Calvinists point to texts in which God ordains evil acts for good purposes while the agents remain guilty (Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23; Acts 4:27-28), and argue that Molinism faces a parallel question since God knowingly actualises a world in which specific people sin and perish.
6043: Calvinists answer that they too warn against prying into the secret decree and direct believers to Christ (Calvin called Christ the mirror of election), but hold that Scripture itself speaks of God's choosing some and hardening others (Rom 9:18), so silence on reprobation would be less than biblical.
6044: Calvinists acknowledge Greek patristic emphasis on free will, but argue that many Fathers were opposing pagan fatalism and Gnostic determinism rather than addressing the Pelagian question, and that Scripture, not consensus of a subset of Fathers, is the final norm.
6045: Calvinists answer that Eph 2:5 says God made us alive while we were dead, which is God's act, and that the grammar of 2:8 most naturally treats the whole salvation package, including faith, as God's gift; John 1:13 and 1 John 5:1 tie new birth to God's will and place it before believing.
6046: Calvinists hold that the offer is sincere because every hearer who believes will certainly be saved and the offer reflects God's real delight in repentance. Faithful Reformed preaching has historically been fervently evangelistic (Whitefield, Spurgeon, William Carey).
6047: Calvinists believe God drags unwilling people into heaven kicking and screaming.
6048: Reformed theology teaches that regeneration renews the will so that people come to Christ freely and gladly; 'irresistible' means effectual, not coercive (Canons of Dort 3/4.11–12).
6050: Calvinists believe God ordains means as well as ends, so preaching is the instrument by which he calls the elect; historic Calvinists founded major missionary movements (e.g. William Carey's Baptist Missionary Society, 1792).
6051: Calvinists deny human choice and responsibility.
6052: The Westminster Confession (ch. 9) affirms that humans have natural liberty and act willingly; Calvinism is compatibilist, not fatalist, and holds people fully accountable for their sin.
6053: Grounds assurance in God's faithfulness rather than human performance.
6054: Fosters humility and doxology: salvation is all of grace.
6055: Produced a large body of rigorous exegesis, confessions and catechisms (Westminster, Heidelberg, 1689).
6056: Historically fuelled missions and revival preaching (Whitefield, Edwards, Carey, Spurgeon).
6057: Can produce anxiety about whether one is elect, a recurring pastoral problem in Puritan history.
6058: Hyper-Calvinist fringes have at times discouraged free offers of the gospel.
6059: Critics argue it raises acute theodicy problems and can portray God as arbitrary.
6060: Debates over TULIP have divided congregations and denominations, notably in modern Baptist life.
6061: Augustine (in his late works) and the medieval Augustinian tradition (Gottschalk, Thomas Bradwardine, Gregory of Rimini) in related forms
6062: Reformed and Presbyterian churches (Westminster Confession, Three Forms of Unity)
6063: Particular Baptists and Reformed Baptists (Second London Confession, 1689)
6064: Puritans such as William Perkins, John Owen, Thomas Goodwin
6065: George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards, Charles Spurgeon
6066: Modern figures: J. I. Packer, R. C. Sproul, John Piper, Timothy Keller, Thomas Schreiner
6067: Today: PCA, OPC, Reformed churches worldwide, a significant minority in the Southern Baptist Convention, many churches in Korea, Africa and Latin America
6069:
Arminianism agrees with Calvinism that fallen humans cannot turn to God unaided, but holds that God, by prevenient (enabling) grace given through the gospel and the Spirit, restores to all who hear the ability to believe or refuse. God elects to salvation those who believe in Christ: either individuals whose faith he foreknows, or Christ and the body of believers as a corporate people. Christ died for every person, grace can be resisted, and (in classical Arminianism) a believer can finally fall away by abandoning faith.

Its defenders stress that this account best honours God's universal love, the sincerity of the gospel offer, and genuine moral responsibility, while still attributing salvation wholly to grace.
6071: Dutch Reformed pastor and Leiden professor
6072: Trained at Leiden and in Geneva under Beza, Arminius became a pastor in Amsterdam and professor at Leiden. Studying Romans 7 and 9 he came to doubt the Reformed doctrine of unconditional reprobation. He affirmed total depravity and the necessity of grace, but taught that God elects believers in Christ, foreknowing who will believe, and that grace can be resisted. He died before the controversy reached its climax.
6074: Remonstrant theologian, leader at the Synod of Dort
6075: Leading spokesman of the Remonstrants, who were expelled from the Synod of Dort. He drafted the Remonstrant Confession and later taught at the Remonstrant seminary in Amsterdam, giving Arminian theology a systematic shape.
6078: Evangelist whose preaching and organisation of Methodist societies spread an evangelical Arminianism across Britain and North America. He emphasised prevenient grace, universal atonement, assurance by the witness of the Spirit and growth toward entire sanctification, and broke with George Whitefield over predestination.
6081: Baptist theologian and historian, Baylor University
